questions.scenario: A request with a valid access token for a customer calls an admin-only endpoint.
questions.question: Which status should the API return?
options: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found in every case
403 Forbidden: the caller is authenticated but not authorised
401 Unauthorized: the caller is not authenticated
questions.explanation: 401 means 'who are you?' has not been answered. Here identity is proven but the permission is missing, which is 403.

questions.scenario: A configuration contains, in this order: requestMatchers("/api/**").permitAll(), then requestMatchers("/api/v1/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN"), then anyRequest().authenticated().
questions.question: Who can call /api/v1/admin/users?
options: Nobody
Any authenticated user
Only ADMIN users
Anyone, including anonymous callers, because the first matching rule (/api/**) permits all
questions.explanation: Spring Security evaluates request rules in order and the first match wins. The broad permitAll rule shadows the admin rule; specific rules must come first.

questions.scenario: A REST API authenticates every request with an Authorization: Bearer header and creates no sessions or cookies.
questions.question: Is it acceptable to disable CSRF protection for this API?
options: Yes, because HTTPS prevents CSRF
No, because JWTs are cookies
No: CSRF protection must always be enabled
Yes: CSRF exploits credentials the browser attaches automatically, such as cookies, and browsers do not add the Authorization header to cross-site requests by themselves
questions.explanation: CSRF relies on ambient credentials. Bearer tokens sent explicitly by client code are not ambient, so token-based APIs commonly disable it. Cookie-based web apps must keep it.

questions.scenario: A developer configures CORS with allowedOrigins("*") and says the API is now 'protected by CORS'.
questions.question: What is wrong with this statement?
options: CORS only applies to GET requests
CORS replaces authentication
CORS only controls which browser pages may read responses; it does not stop curl, servers or attackers' scripts from calling the API
Nothing: CORS is a server-side access-control mechanism
questions.explanation: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy for chosen origins. Access control must come from authentication and authorisation, and the wildcard origin should not be used for authenticated APIs.

questions.scenario: You want a new endpoint that a colleague forgets to configure to be protected automatically.
questions.question: Which rule achieves this?
options: Annotate each controller with @Secured
Rely on CORS
End the rule list with anyRequest().permitAll()
End the rule list with anyRequest().authenticated() (or denyAll())
questions.explanation: A deny-by-default final rule means anything not explicitly opened requires authentication.

questions.scenario: You are writing tests for a secured transfer endpoint with MockMvc.
questions.question: Which tests are important to include? (Choose two.)
options: A test that the response is 200 for every caller
A token lacking the required scope returns 403
A test that disables security to check the controller logic only
A request with no credentials returns 401
questions.explanation: Negative tests prove that protection works. Tests with security disabled say nothing about access control.

questions.scenario: Your service needs HTTP Basic for /actuator/** (used by the operations team) and JWT bearer tokens for /api/**.
questions.question: How do you configure this cleanly?
options: Two SecurityFilterChain beans with different securityMatcher settings
One chain that accepts both everywhere
Run Actuator in a separate application
Disable security for Actuator
questions.explanation: Each SecurityFilterChain applies to the requests matched by its securityMatcher, so different parts of the application can use different authentication mechanisms and rules.
